topic: Fairness in Topology: The Borsuk-Ulam Theorem and the Stolen Necklace Problem
target_audience: Undergraduate students in Mathematics or Computer Science

sections.title: The Hook: The Disputed Treasure
lecture_lines: Alice and Bob must share a precious stolen necklace.
It contains ten red and eight green beads.
How many cuts ensure each gets a fair split?
animations: Alice (#FFD700) and Bob (#87CEEB) icons appear with a necklace of 10 red (#FF0000) and 8 green (#00FF00) beads.
The necklace is labeled 'Stolen Necklace' and beads are counted: '10 Red, 8 Green'.
A question mark appears next to a knife: 'How many cuts for a fair split?'.

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Intermediate Value Theorem (1D Case)
lecture_lines: Slide a knife along a necklace of one type.
Alice's share changes continuously from zero to total.
The Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees a perfect 50/50 split.
animations: A single string of red beads (#FF0000) is shown with a sliding white cut line moving left to right.
A plot appears showing Alice's share (%) of red beads increasing from 0% to 100% as the line moves.
The plot hits the 50% mark, and the point is highlighted in yellow (#FFFF00) to illustrate the IVT.

sections.title: The Core Concept: The Borsuk-Ulam Theorem
lecture_lines: Antipodal points are exactly opposite each other on spheres.
The Borsuk-Ulam theorem states their function values match.
Two opposite Earth locations share temperature and pressure.
animations: A sphere (S2) appears with two red dots (#FF0000) at antipodal positions labeled x and -x.
The mathematical formula f(x) = f(-x) appears in white (#FFFFFF) at the top of the screen.
The sphere represents Earth, showing two opposite points with matching 'Temp: 20C' and 'Press: 1013hPa'.

sections.title: Mapping the Necklace to a Sphere
lecture_lines: Represent necklace cuts as points on a circular loop.
Each sphere location corresponds to a specific cut configuration.
Antipodal points on the sphere represent swapping all portions.
animations: The necklace is shown, then transformed into a circular loop (S1) to represent the space of cuts.
A point on a sphere is highlighted, labeled 'Cut Positions', representing a specific partition.
The antipodal point is shown, and the necklace segments swap colors between Alice (#FFD700) and Bob (#87CEEB).

sections.title: The Elegant Solution
lecture_lines: Map the sphere to the space of bead amounts.
Borsuk-Ulam identifies a point where both shares match.
This guarantees a perfect 50/50 split for every type.
animations: A 2D coordinate system (R2) represents Alice's share of two types of beads (Red and Green).
A mapping from the sphere to R2 shows two antipodal points mapping to the same (0.5, 0.5) coordinate.
The cuts on the necklace shift to the positions that yield exactly 50% of each bead type for both parties.

sections.title: Conclusion and Real-World Intuition
lecture_lines: For k bead types, only k cuts are required.
Topology provides an elegant solution to fair resource allocation.
The Borsuk-Ulam Theorem makes the impossible division possible.
animations: Text 'k beads, k cuts' appears in bold white (#FFFFFF) to summarize the general result.
Alice and Bob icons appear holding their equal shares of the necklace, looking satisfied.
A final zoom out shows the necklace and sphere overlay as a cohesive mathematical summary.
